claim: Antibiotic resistance is a worldwide challenge.
source: Antibiotic resistance is a worldwide challenge.
evidence: This is a general statement about the global nature of antibiotic resistance, representing established scientific consensus.

claim: CD15-3 inhibits WT DHFR and its TMP resistant variants L28R, P21L and A26T with IC50 50–75 µM against WT and TMP-resistant strains.
source: We identified a novel compound (CD15-3) that inhibits WT DHFR and its TMP resistant variants L28R, P21L and A26T with IC50 50–75 µM against WT and TMP-resistant strains.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of IC50 values reported in the manuscript.

claim: Resistance to CD15-3 was dramatically delayed compared to TMP in in vitro evolution.
source: Resistance to CD15-3 was dramatically delayed compared to TMP in in vitro evolution.
evidence: This is supported by experimental evolution data comparing CD15-3 and TMP resistance development.

claim: Whole genome sequencing of CD15-3-resistant strains showed no mutations in the target folA locus.
source: Whole genome sequencing of CD15-3-resistant strains showed no mutations in the target folA locus.
evidence: This is directly supported by whole genome sequencing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Gene duplication of several efflux pumps gave rise to weak (about twofold increase in IC50) resistance against CD15-3.
source: Rather, gene duplication of several efflux pumps gave rise to weak (about twofold increase in IC50) resistance against CD15-3.
evidence: This is supported by whole genome sequencing data and IC50 measurements of evolved strains.

claim: ESKAPE pathogens include Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Enterobacter spp.
source: Emergence of these 'superbugs' including ESKAPE (Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Enterobacter spp.) (Peneş et al., 2017) call for novel approaches to design antibiotic compounds that act as 'evolution drugs' by blocking evolutionary escape from antibiotic stressor.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Peneş et al., 2017.

claim: Current drug development protocols and treatment strategies have limited success in addressing the issue of drug resistance.
source: Currently, drug development protocols and treatment strategies have limited success in addressing the issue of drug resistance as it overlooks the driving complex underlying evolutionary selection processes.
evidence: This represents a general assessment based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: DHFR plays a critical role in nucleotide biosynthesis.
source: Dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) is one such protein, which, due to its critical role in nucleotide biosynthesis, has been a central antibacterial and anticancer drug target (Lin and Bertino, 1991; Schweitzer et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lin and Bertino, 1991 and Schweitzer et al., 1990.

claim: Classical DHFR inhibitors generally contain a 2,4-diamino-1,3-diaza pharmacophore group.
source: The classical DHFR inhibitors generally contain a 2,4-diamino-1,3-diaza pharmacophore group (Srinivasan et al., 2017) which constitute structural analogues of its substrate dihydrofolate and competitively bind the receptor-DHFR active site.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Srinivasan et al., 2017.

claim: Methotrexate (MTX) is approved as an anticancer drug.
source: Inhibitors of this type such as methotrexate (MTX) (Bleyer, 2015) and pralatrexate (PDX) (Izbicka et al., 2009) are approved as anticancer drugs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bleyer, 2015.

claim: Trimethoprim (TMP) is approved as an antibacterial drug.
source: Non-classical antifolate drugs like trimethoprim (TMP)(Finland and Kass, 1973) trimetotrexate (TMQ) (Lin and Bertino, 1991), that interact selectively with bacterial but not human DHFR are approved as antibacterial drugs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Finland and Kass, 1973.

claim: Point mutations in critical amino acid residues of the binding cavity represent an important mode of trimethoprim resistance.
source: In general, both clinical and in vitro studies have shown that accumulation of point mutations in critical amino acids residues of the binding cavity represent an important mode of trimethoprim resistance.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from clinical and in vitro studies.

claim: Point mutations conferring resistance in bacteria to anti-DHFR compounds are primarily located in the folA locus that encodes DHFR in E. coli.
source: Point mutations conferring resistance in bacteria to anti-DHFR compounds are primarily located in the folA locus that encodes DHFR in E. coli (Oz et al., 2014; Tamer et al., 2019; Toprak et al., 2012) making DHFR an appealing target to develop evolution antibiotic drugs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Oz et al., 2014; Tamer et al., 2019; Toprak et al., 2012.

claim: The closed conformation of M20 loop (PDB 1RX3) was adopted as the most representative crystal structure for the initial SBVS of compound databases.
source: Therefore, the closed conformation of M20 loop (PDB 1RX3) was adopted as the most representative crystal structure for the initial SBVS of compound databases for novel broad range inhibitors.
evidence: This is based on computational analysis comparing docking scores with experimental binding affinities.

claim: Using the closed conformation of M20 loop (PDB 1RX3), the largest proportion of known inhibitors was recovered.
source: Using the closed conformation of M20 loop (PDB 1RX3), we were able to recover the largest proportion of known inhibitors (Table 2 and Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 2 and Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: A total of 307 candidate compounds with strongest docking score that form hydrogen bond with the critical residue Asp27 in the DHFR-binding pocket were submitted for more accurate prediction of binding free energy.
source: A total of 307 candidate compounds with strongest docking score that form hydrogen bond with the critical residue Asp27 in the DHFR-binding pocket, were submitted for more accurate prediction of binding free energy (Cheron and Shakhnovich, 2017; Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the computational screening workflow shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The models reproduced known binding affinities with high accuracy.
source: The models reproduced known binding affinities with high accuracy (see Figure 1B and C and Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B, C and supplementary figures.

claim: Asp27 forms hydrogen bond with almost all DHFR inhibitors in the ligand-binding cavity.
source: Further, the analysis of the DHFR crystal structures showed that Asp27 forms hydrogen bond with almost all DHFR inhibitors in the ligand-binding cavity.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of DHFR crystal structures.

claim: A total of 40 prospective active compounds were purchased for evaluation.
source: Altogether, a total of 40 prospective active compounds were purchased for evaluation.
evidence: This describes the experimental workflow.

claim: A total of 13, 8, 6, and 14 compounds resulted in more than 20% loss of the DHFR catalytic activity at 200 µM concentration for WT, P21L, A26T, and L28R DHFR, respectively.
source: As shown in Figure 2A-B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, a total of 13, 8, 6, and 14 compounds resulted in more than 20% loss of the DHFR catalytic activity at that concentration for WT, P21L, A26T, and L28R DHFR, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Compounds CD15, CD17, and CD08 showed more than 30% inhibition against both WT and all three DHFR mutants.
source: Among them, compounds CD15, CD17, and CD08 showed more than 30% inhibition against both WT and all three DHFR mutants (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: For compound CD15, the Ki values were all less than 5 μM against WT and three single-point DHFR mutants.
source: For compound CD15, the Ki values were all less than 5 μM against WT and three single-point DHFR mutants.
evidence: This is supported by experimental Ki measurements reported in Table 1.

claim: For the L28R mutant, the Ki values for CD15 were 1.0 μM, outperforming the WT, P21L, or A26T mutant DHFR.
source: For the L28R mutant, the Ki values were 1.0 μM, outperforming the WT, P21L, or A26T mutant DHFR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental Ki measurements reported in Table 1.

claim: L28R is a strong TMP escape variant.
source: It is worth noting that L28R is a strong TMP escape variant (Rodrigues et al., 2016; Toprak et al., 2012), thus the discovered CD15 series appeared a promising candidate for an 'evolution drug' that has a potential to suppress even most intractable escape variants.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rodrigues et al., 2016 and Toprak et al., 2012.

claim: Both CD15 and CD17 showed similar inhibition against WT DHFR from L.grayi and C.muridarum.
source: We found that both compounds showed similar inhibition against the two species (see Figure 3 and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: CD15 is approximately as active or better against double resistant mutants than against single mutants.
source: We also evaluated inhibitory activity of CD15 against double resistant mutants and found that they are approximately as active or better than against single mutants (see Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: IC50 of TMP for E. coli strain with chromosomal L28R DHFR is about 80 times higher than of WT.
source: In particular, IC50 of TMP for E. coli strain with chromosomal L28R DHFR is about 80 times higher than of WT (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 2.

claim: Both CD15 and CD17 inhibit growth of the WT and three single folA mutant E. coli strains.
source: As shown in Figure 4A and B, dose-response curves clearly demonstrated that both CD15 and CD17 inhibit growth of the WT and three single folA mutant E. coli strains.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: In terms of IC50, CD15 is comparable with TMP on the most resistant variant L28R.
source: Importantly, in terms of IC50 CD15 is comparable with TMP on the most resistant variant L28R.
evidence: This is based on comparison of IC50 values from experimental data.

claim: CD15-3 showed about 2.4-fold better efficacy than that of TMP on L28R E. coli variant strain.
source: CD15-3 showed about 2.4-fold better efficacy than that of TMP on L28R E. coli variant strain (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: No inhibitory activity for CD15-3 was detected against human DHFR.
source: As shown in Table 1 no inhibitory activity for CD15-3 was detected against human DHFR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: The lack of inhibition on human DHFR for CD15-3 can be attributed to the loss of the pi-pi interaction with Phe31.
source: The lack of inhibition on human DHFR for CD15-3 can be attributed to the loss of the pi-pi interaction with Phe31.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis comparing E. coli and human DHFR.

claim: Both CD15 and CD15-3 formed two hydrogen bonds with the key residue Asp27 by the hydroxy group in the 6-hydroxy-3-methylpyrimidine-2,4 (1H,3H)-dione scaffold.
source: As shown in Figure 5B and C, both compounds formed two hydrogen bonds with the key residue Asp27 by the hydroxy group in the 6-hydroxy-3-methylpyrimidine-2,4 (1H,3H)-dione scaffold.
evidence: This is supported by molecular docking analysis shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Overexpression of WT DHFR using pBAD-promoter and at 0.005% arabinose induction showed improvement in growth rates compared to WT cells with empty pBAD-plasmid under conditions of CD15-3 treatment.
source: Interestingly, controlled expression of folA (encoding DHFR) under pBAD promoter with 0.005% arabinose induction partially rescued growth in a certain range of CD15-3 concentrations (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: No growth recovery from CD15-3-induced inhibition was observed upon overexpression of the inactive DHFR variant D27F.
source: We found that no growth recovery from CD15-3-induced inhibition upon overexpression of the inactive DHFR variant.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Growth of CD15-3-treated cells was partially rescued by folA mix.
source: We found that growth of CD15-3-treated cells was partially rescued by folA mix and again the effect was more prominent at relatively lower concentrations of CD15-3 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: At early stages of evolution, the CD15-3 concentration necessary to reduce the growth rate of the culture to 50% increased to a value about 2.7 times higher than the IC50 of the naïve strain.
source: We found that, at early stages of evolution, the CD15-3 concentration necessary to reduce the growth rate of the culture to 50% (with respect to non-inhibited naïve cells) increased to a value about 2.7 times higher than the IC50 of the naïve strain.
evidence: This is supported by experimental evolution data.

claim: At the end of the evolutionary experiment, the cells evolved TMP resistance with IC50 between 8- and 200-fold higher than original naïve E. coli strain.
source: At the end of the evolutionary experiment, the cells evolved TMP resistance with IC50 between 8- and 200-fold higher than original naïve E. coli strain (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental evolution data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Sanger sequencing of the folA locus revealed point mutations in the folA locus in all TMP evolution trajectories.
source: Sanger sequencing of the folA locus revealed point mutations in the folA locus in all trajectories.
evidence: This is supported by Sanger sequencing data.

claim: No mutations at or upstream of the folA locus was found in CD15-3 evolved strains.
source: No mutations at or upstream of the folA locus was found.
evidence: This is supported by whole genome sequencing data.

claim: The duplicated segment in the genome of the evolved variant contained genes encoding porin proteins, ABC transporter permeases and cation efflux pump genes (cus-genes).
source: The duplicated segment in the genome of the evolved variant contained genes encoding porin proteins, ABC transporter permeases and cation efflux pump genes (cus-genes) (Supplementary file 2: Duplicated genome stretch).
evidence: This is supported by whole genome sequencing data.

claim: The abundance of CD15-3 was found to be around 10% of the initial abundance after 4 hr of CD15-3 treatment in evolved strains.
source: After 4 hr of CD15-3 treatment, the abundance of the drug was found to be around 10% of the initial abundance.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS metabolic characterization data.

claim: CD15-3-evolved cells showed about threefold higher IC50 for TMP and Sulphamethoxazole.
source: Under both treatment conditions, CD15-3-evolved cells partially escaped the drug inhibition and showed about threefold higher IC50 for TMP and Sulphamethoxazole (Figure 8D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D and E.

claim: Treated WT cells showed a wide distribution of cell length with a median length which was more than double than that of the untreated sets.
source: Treated cells showed a wide distribution of cell length with a median length which was more than double than that of the untreated sets (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is supported by DIC imaging data shown in Figure 9E.

claim: Evolved cells after CD15-3 treatment had a median cell length of 1.26 µm which is slightly higher than that of untreated set.
source: Evolved cells after CD15-3 treatment had a median cell length of 1.26 µm which is slightly higher than that of untreated set.
evidence: This is supported by DIC imaging data shown in Figure 9E.

claim: The M20 loop in DHFR has three major types of conformation (open, closed and occluded) that are important for catalysis.
source: In the crystal structures of E. coli DHFR, the M20 loop (residues 9–24) has three major types of conformation (open, closed and occluded) (Falzone et al., 1994) that are important for catalysis.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Falzone et al., 1994.

claim: The closed conformation of M20 loop is adopted when the substrate and cofactor are both bound.
source: It has shown that the closed conformation is adopted when the substrate and cofactor are both bound (Agarwal et al., 2002), where the M20 loop is packed against the nicotinamide ring of the cofactor.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Agarwal et al., 2002.

claim: The closed conformation is the only conformation where substrate and cofactor are arranged favorably for reaction.
source: This is the only conformation where substrate and cofactor are arranged favorably for reaction and the following state of the catalytic cycle (Agarwal et al., 2002) and also the only conformation that can be found in DHFR from all other species, regardless of the crystal packing and ligands bound positions in the binding site (Sawaya and Kraut, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Agarwal et al., 2002 and Sawaya and Kraut, 1997.

claim: The occluded M20 loop is an unproductive conformation in which the central part of the M20 loop forms a helix that blocks access to the binding site for the nicotinamide moiety of the cofactor.
source: Observed in the product complexes, the occluded M20 loop is an unproductive conformation in which the central part of the M20 loop forms a helix that blocks access to the binding site for the nicotinamide moiety of the cofactor.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of DHFR crystal structures.

claim: The Pearson correlation coefficient (R) between the predicted and experimental binding free energies for eight known E. coli DHFR inhibitors was 0.942.
source: Two replicates of 10 ns simulation provided a quite strong correlation (R = 0.942) between the computational and experimental binding free energies (Figure 1B)
evidence: This is supported by computational and experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The correlation coefficient (R) for TMP against WT DHFR and seven resistant DHFR mutants was 0.953.
source: The reason why the prediction for L. grayi and C. muridarum is somewhat inferior to E. coli DHFR (R = 0.953 from Figure 1C in the manuscript)
evidence: This is supported by computational and experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The correlation coefficient (R) for L. grayi DHFR was 0.895.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7, from two replicates of 10 ns simulation, the correlation coefficient (R) for L. grayi and C. muridarum DHFR were 0.895 and 0.839, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by computational and experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: The correlation coefficient (R) for C. muridarum DHFR was 0.839.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7, from two replicates of 10 ns simulation, the correlation coefficient (R) for L. grayi and C. muridarum DHFR were 0.895 and 0.839, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by computational and experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: All six CD17 series compounds did not pass the PAINS test.
source: All six CD17 series compounds did not pass the PAINS test and therefore were not considered for further analysis.
evidence: This is based on computational PAINS filter analysis.

claim: TMP forms hydrogen bond with Ile94 as well as the conserved water molecule HOH302.
source: However, in addition to the hydrogen bond formed with Asp27, TMP also forms hydrogen bond with another critical residue Ile94 as well as the conserved water molecule HOH302.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of TMP-DHFR complexes.

claim: Naphthalene group of CD15-3 extends further in DHFR binding pocket than the corresponding trimethoxybenzene of TMP.
source: Naphthalene group of CD15-3 extends further in DHFR binding pocket than the corresponding trimethoxybenzene of TMP, potentially resulting in additional hydrophobic interaction with L28R in DHFR which provides structural rationale for strong potency of CD15-3 against resistant L28R variant.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and provides a mechanistic explanation.

claim: Overexpression of WT DHFR rescued growth of TMP-treated cells.
source: Overexpression of WT DHFR rescued growth of TMP-treated cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: No rescue of growth from TMP-induced inhibition was observed upon overexpression of inactive D27F variant.
source: while no rescue of growth from TMP-induced inhibition was observed upon overexpression of inactive D27F variant (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: DHFR is an intracellular target for the new compound CD15-3.
source: These results indicate that DHFR is an intracellular target for the new compound CD15-3.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple lines of experimental evidence including overexpression and metabolic supplementation studies.

claim: CD15-3 might inhibit other proteins besides DHFR at high concentrations.
source: At the same time, we observed only partial rescue of CD15-3 inhibited growth by folA mix or DHFR complementation at higher concentrations of CD15-3 suggesting that at high concentrations this compound might inhibit other proteins besides DHFR.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of only partial rescue at high CD15-3 concentrations.

claim: None of the colonies that grew on CD15-3 plates showed mutation in the folA locus.
source: None of the colonies that grew on CD15-3 plates showed mutation in the folA locus (Table 3)
evidence: This is supported by Sanger sequencing data shown in Table 3.

claim: 10 of the 18 colonies isolated from the TMP plate showed mutations in the folA locus.
source: while 10 of the 18 colonies isolated from the TMP plate showed mutations in the folA locus.
evidence: This is supported by Sanger sequencing data shown in Table 3.

claim: The colonies formed on the CD15-3 plate had IC50 values roughly 1.7–2.3 times higher than against WT.
source: The colonies formed on the CD15-3 plate had IC50 values roughly 1.7–2.3 times higher than against WT (Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental IC50 measurements shown in Table 3.

claim: The duplicated segment was found to be a stretch of above 81 KB.
source: The duplicated segment was found to be a stretch of above 81 KB.
evidence: This is supported by whole genome sequencing data.

claim: The CusCFBA system is a HME (heavy metal efflux)-RND system identified in E. coli.
source: The CusCFBA system is a HME (heavy metal efflux)-RND system identified in E. coli.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about bacterial efflux systems.

claim: Cus-efflux system was initially identified for the extrusion of silver (Ag+) and copper (Cu+).
source: Cus-efflux system was initially identified for the extrusion of silver (Ag+) and copper (Cu+).
evidence: This represents established knowledge about the Cus-efflux system.

claim: Cus-efflux system has been found to induce resistance to fosfomycin, dinitrophenol, dinitrobenzene, and ethionamide.
source: They have been found to induce resistance to fosfomycin (Nishino and Yamaguchi, 2001), dinitrophenol, dinitrobenzene, and ethionamide (Coutinho et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nishino and Yamaguchi, 2001 and Coutinho et al., 2010.

claim: CD15-3 inhibited the D27E TMP escape mutants along with P21L mutant with IC50 close to naïve WT strain.
source: Interestingly CD15-3 inhibited the D27E TMP escape mutants along with P21L mutant with IC50 close to naïve WT strain (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: IC50 for W30R and W30C TMP escape mutants against CD15-3 is less than twofold higher compared to that of WT.
source: Still IC50 for these TMP escape mutants against CD15-3 is less than twofold higher compared to that of WT.
evidence: This is supported by experimental IC50 measurements.

claim: Untreated WT (naive) and evolved cells had comparable cell lengths with median cell lengths of 1.07 µm.
source: Untreated WT (naive) and evolved cells had comparable cell lengths with median cell lengths of 1.07 µm. (n.s. indicates the distribution of cell lengths were not significantly different, Mann-Whitney test, p-value = 0.961).
evidence: This is supported by DIC imaging data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 9E.

claim: WT-treated cells were observed to have a filamentous morphology and the median cell length (2.34 µm.) double of that of the untreated WT set.
source: WT-treated cells were observed to have a filamentous morphology and the median cell length (2.34 µm.) double of that of the untreated WT set.
evidence: This is supported by DIC imaging data shown in Figure 9E.

claim: The cell size distribution of the evolved cells showed much less change after CD15-3 treatment compared to that observed for the WT.
source: But the cell size distribution of the evolved cells showed much less change after CD15-3 treatment compared to that observed for the WT (* indicates the distribution of cell lengths were significantly different, Mann-Whitney test, p-value < 0.001).
evidence: This is supported by DIC imaging data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 9E.

claim: Efflux genes comprise 38% of the duplicated genome segment.
source: As efflux genes comprise 38 % of the duplicated genome segment (Supplementary file 2: Duplicated genome stretch)
evidence: This is supported by whole genome sequencing data analysis.

claim: L28R mutation is stabilizing showing an increase in Tm of 6°C above WT DHFR.
source: Thermal denaturation experiments demonstrate that L28R mutation is stabilizing showing an increase in Tm of 6°C above WT DHFR, in contrast to the destabilizing mutations P21L and A26T (Rodrigues et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rodrigues et al., 2016.

claim: The L28R mutation cancels out the destabilization brought by P21L and A26T, restoring the Tm of the double and triple mutants to WT values.
source: In addition, the L28R mutation cancels out the destabilization brought by P21L and A26T, restoring the Tm of the double and triple mutants to WT values.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rodrigues et al., 2016.

claim: The L28R mutation shows improved compactness, inferred from its reduced bis-ANS binding.
source: The L28R mutation also shows improved compactness, inferred from its reduced bis-ANS binding (Rodrigues et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rodrigues et al., 2016.

claim: L28R serves as a stability 'reservoir' providing a gateway to multiple evolutionary trajectories leading to resistance.
source: Effectively L28R serves as a stability 'reservoir' providing a gateway to multiple evolutionary trajectories leading to resistance.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the biophysical properties of L28R and its role in resistance evolution.

claim: Cellular filamentation and concomitant morphological changes are one of the visible hallmarks of stress responses to inhibition of proteins on the folate pathway.
source: As cellular filamentation and concomitant morphological changes are one of the visible hallmarks of stress responses to inhibition of proteins on the folate pathway of which DHFR is a member,(Ahmad et al., 1998; Justice et al., 2008; Sangurdekar et al., 2011; Zaritsky et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ahmad et al., 1998; Justice et al., 2008; Sangurdekar et al., 2011; Zaritsky et al., 2006.

claim: Horizontal gene transfer is a critical mechanism conferring antibiotic resistance in bacterial population.
source: Horizontal gene transfer – another critical mechanism conferring antibiotic resistance (Dzidic and Bedeković, 2003) in bacterial population – presents further complications.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dzidic and Bedeković, 2003.

claim: Natural product antibiotics like penicillin and other beta lactam drugs are inherently multi-target antibiotics.
source: It is interesting to note that natural product antibiotics like penicillin and other beta lactam drugs are inherently multi-target antibiotics (Tyers and Wright, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tyers and Wright, 2019.

claim: Tetracyclin and aminoglycosides target bacterial ribosome and interact with multiple ribosomal proteins.
source: Same applies to tetracyclin and aminoglycosides which targets bacterial ribosome and in turn interact with multiple ribosomal proteins (Forge and Schacht, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Forge and Schacht, 2000.

claim: E. coli cells evolved in the presence of trimethoprim can become virtually insensitive to the drug upon successive accumulation of mutations in target gene.
source: Several studies have shown that E. coli cells evolved in the presence of trimethoprim, a DHFR inhibitor, can become virtually insensitive to the drug upon successive accumulation of mutations in target gene.
evidence: This represents established knowledge from multiple studies.

claim: P21L, A26T, L28R mutations and their combinations recurrently appeared in two out of five independent evolution experiments.
source: Among trimethoprim-resistant mutations, P21L, A26T, L28R, and their combinations recurrently appeared in two out of five independent evolution experiments, and their order of fixation in both cases was similar (Toprak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Toprak et al., 2012.

claim: Introduction of another mutation on the L28R background, either P21L or A26T, does not change IC50 significantly.
source: Introduction of another mutation on the L28R background, either P21L or A26T, does not change IC50 significantly (Rodrigues et al., 2016; Toprak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rodrigues et al., 2016 and Toprak et al., 2012.
